blocks.prompt: 3 (i) If \(A\) and \(B\) are square matrices of the same order, then explain why in general: \((A + B)^2 \neq A^2 + 2AB + B^2\).
blocks.explanation:
This asks for a reason, not a calculation: why the familiar algebra identity can fail for matrices.
We must expand \((A + B)^2\) carefully, keeping the order of every product, and see what extra condition the identity needs.
Plan: expand, compare with \(A^2 + 2AB + B^2\), then show one pair of matrices where the two sides differ.
steps:
Given: \(A\), \(B\) square matrices of the same order (so \(A + B\), \(AB\), \(BA\) all exist).
To explain: why in general \((A + B)^2 \neq A^2 + 2AB + B^2\).
Method: Expand using the distributive law, never swapping the order of a product, because matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.

Write the square as a product and expand
\[(A + B)^2 = (A + B)(A + B)\]
\[= A(A + B) + B(A + B)\]
\[= A^2 + AB + BA + B^2\]
Why: The distributive law holds for matrices. In \(B(A + B)\) the \(B\) stays on the left, so we get \(BA\), not \(AB\).

Compare with the formula
\[AB + BA = 2AB \iff BA = AB\]
Why: The two sides match only when the middle terms match. In numbers \(ba = ab\) always, but for matrices \(BA\) and \(AB\) are in general different.

Show one example where they differ
\[A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\; B = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
\[AB = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\; BA = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Here \(AB \neq BA\), so the identity should fail.

Work out both sides for this example
\[A + B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
\[(A + B)^2 = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
\[A^2 + 2AB + B^2 = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: \(A^2 = A\), \(B^2 = O\) and \(2AB\) has 2 in place (1, 2). The two results differ in entry (1, 2), so the identity is false here.

Conclusion
Why: The identity is true only for matrices with \(AB = BA\) (for example \(B = I\) or \(B = A\)). Since this is not true in general, \((A + B)^2 \neq A^2 + 2AB + B^2\) in general.
blocks.final_answer: \((A + B)^2 = A^2 + AB + BA + B^2\), which equals \(A^2 + 2AB + B^2\) only when \(AB = BA\); since \(AB \neq BA\) in general, the identity fails in general.

blocks.prompt: 3 (ii) If \(A\) and \(B\) are square matrices of the same order, then explain why in general: \((A - B)^2 \neq A^2 - 2AB + B^2\).
blocks.explanation:
The same question as (i), now with a minus sign.
We must expand \((A - B)^2\) keeping the order of products and find the condition the identity needs.
Plan: expand, compare, then test with the same example as (i).
steps:
Given: \(A\), \(B\) square matrices of the same order.
To explain: why in general \((A - B)^2 \neq A^2 - 2AB + B^2\).
Method: Expand with the distributive law, keeping every product in its order.

Expand
\[(A - B)^2 = (A - B)(A - B)\]
\[= A(A - B) - B(A - B)\]
\[= A^2 - AB - BA + B^2\]
Why: The minus in front of \(B(A - B)\) changes both signs: \(-BA + B^2\).

Compare with the formula
\[-AB - BA = -2AB \iff BA = AB\]
Why: Only the middle terms differ, and they agree only when \(AB = BA\).

Test with the example of part (i)
\[A - B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
\[(A - B)^2 = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
\[A^2 - 2AB + B^2 = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: With \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\) we have \(AB \neq BA\), and the two sides differ in entry (1, 2).

Conclusion
Why: The identity holds only when \(AB = BA\), which is not true in general.
blocks.final_answer: \((A - B)^2 = A^2 - AB - BA + B^2\), which equals \(A^2 - 2AB + B^2\) only when \(AB = BA\); so in general the identity fails.

blocks.prompt: 3 (iii) If \(A\) and \(B\) are square matrices of the same order, then explain why in general: \((A + B)(A - B) \neq A^2 - B^2\).
blocks.explanation:
The difference-of-squares identity, tested for matrices.
We must expand \((A + B)(A - B)\) in order and see when the middle terms cancel.
Plan: expand, compare with \(A^2 - B^2\), test with the example from (i).
steps:
Given: \(A\), \(B\) square matrices of the same order.
To explain: why in general \((A + B)(A - B) \neq A^2 - B^2\).
Method: Distributive law, keeping the order of every product.

Expand
\[(A + B)(A - B)\]
\[= A(A - B) + B(A - B)\]
\[= A^2 - AB + BA - B^2\]
Why: \(B(A - B) = BA - B^2\); the \(B\) stays on the left.

Compare with \(A^2 - B^2\)
\[-AB + BA = O \iff BA = AB\]
Why: The middle terms cancel (give the zero matrix) only if \(BA = AB\).

Test with the example of part (i)
\[(A + B)(A - B) = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
\[A^2 - B^2 = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: With \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\): \(A + B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\), \(A - B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\), \(A^2 = A\), \(B^2 = O\). Entry (1, 2) is \(-1\) on one side and 0 on the other.

Conclusion
Why: The middle terms \(-AB + BA\) do not cancel unless \(AB = BA\), so in general \((A + B)(A - B) \neq A^2 - B^2\).
blocks.final_answer: \((A + B)(A - B) = A^2 - AB + BA - B^2\), which equals \(A^2 - B^2\) only when \(AB = BA\); so in general the identity fails.
